16010:
1. The Literal Meaning: The Nail on Your Thumb

Your thumb has a nail growing on it, just like your other fingers. That nail is your thumbnail. It is typically the widest and flattest of all your fingernails, sitting on the broadest of your five fingers.

This is the original, physical meaning of the word — a part of the human body.
2. The Extended Meaning: A Small Preview of Something Larger

Because the thumbnail is physically small, the word stretched over time to describe anything that is a reduced, compact version of something larger — small enough to take in at a glance, but detailed enough to give you an idea of the whole thing.

This gave rise to two important uses:

a. In Digital Media — The Most Common Modern Use

A thumbnail is a small, reduced image that acts as a preview or stand-in for something larger — a full-size photo, a video, a document, or a webpage.

Its job is simple: let you quickly identify what something is before you open or load the full version.

Everyday examples:

  • YouTube: The small picture you see before clicking on a video is called a thumbnail. It gives you a quick idea of what the video is about. Creators design them carefully to attract viewers.
  • Photo gallery on your phone: When your photos appear as a neat grid of small images, each of those small images is a thumbnail. Tapping one opens the full photo.
  • Online shopping: Product listings show small images of each item. Those small images are thumbnails. Clicking one usually shows you the full-size photo.
  • File managers on computers: Sometimes, when you browse folders containing images or videos, the files display tiny previews of their content instead of just a plain icon. Those previews are thumbnails.
  • PDF readers and e-books: A side panel sometimes shows small previews of each page. Those are thumbnails — they help you navigate to the right page quickly.

The key idea: a thumbnail is not the real, full thing. It is a small representative image that points you toward the real thing and helps you decide whether to open it.

b. In Art and Design — A Traditional Use

When artists, illustrators, or graphic designers begin working on something, they often don't jump straight into the final piece. Instead, they sketch out many tiny, rough drawings — very quickly, very small — to explore different ideas for layout, composition, and structure. These tiny planning sketches are called thumbnails.

The logic is the same: they are small, fast, and representative of something that may later be developed into a much larger, detailed work.

A concept artist designing a movie scene, for instance, might fill a page with dozens of tiny thumbnail sketches to figure out which arrangement of characters and objects looks best — before spending hours on the final illustration.

The thread running through all uses of this word is the same idea: something small that stands for or gives you a quick sense of something larger.

Your actual thumbnail — the nail on your thumb — is small. The word borrowed that smallness. A digital thumbnail is a shrunken version of a larger image. An artistic thumbnail is a shrunken version of a larger planned work.

In modern everyday language, "thumbnail" almost always refers to the digital preview image — especially in the context of videos, photos, and files. If someone says "I need to make a thumbnail for my video," they mean the small cover image that appears before the video plays.

• A thumbnail is always a visual thing — it is an image, not a summary in words. (When people describe something in words as "in thumbnail" or "a thumbnail description," they are using a related adjective/adverb form, not the noun.)
  • A thumbnail is specifically a reduced version of a particular thing — not just any small image. A tiny decorative icon is not a thumbnail; a shrunken preview of your specific photo is.
  • Thumbnails are functional by nature — they exist to help you navigate, browse, or decide, not just to decorate.
16011:
When you thump something, you hit it hard enough to produce a heavy, dull sound — not a sharp crack or a light tap, but a deep, solid thud. The word itself almost sounds like what it describes. That heavy, muffled impact is the soul of the word.

Think of knocking on a wooden door — not lightly, but with the side of your fist, firmly. That sound and that action together? That's a thump.

1. To Hit Something or Someone Hard

This is the most direct meaning. You use your fist, a hand, or a blunt object to strike something with force.

  • She thumped the table with her fist to get everyone's attention.
  • He thumped the pillow a few times to make it comfortable.
  • The mechanic thumped the car door to get it unstuck.

Notice that thumping is not delicate. It's a deliberate, forceful action. However, it's not always aggressive — someone can thump your back in a friendly, congratulatory way.

2. To Move Heavily, Making a Loud, Dull Sound With Each Step

When a person or animal moves in a way that each step or movement is heavy and loud, you say they are thumping.

  • The children thumped up the stairs and woke everyone up.
  • The elephant thumped across the dry ground.
  • He thumped around the kitchen, slamming cupboards.

Here, the verb is not about hitting anyone — it's about the quality of the movement. It suggests a lack of lightness or grace.

3. To Fall or Land With a Heavy, Dull Impact

When an object falls or hits a surface and makes a deep, solid sound, you can say it thumped.

  • The heavy book thumped onto the floor.
  • The bag thumped down on the desk.
  • Something thumped against the wall in the next room.

4. To Beat Hard (Especially the Heart)

This is a very common and expressive use. When your heart beats fast and hard — because of fear, excitement, nervousness, or physical effort — it thumps.

  • Her heart thumped wildly as she waited for the results.
  • He could feel his heart thumping in his chest as he ran.
  • My heart thumped the moment I heard the strange noise.

This usage captures the physical sensation of an intense heartbeat — you can almost feel it hitting your ribcage.

5. To Defeat Someone Decisively (Mainly British, Informal)

In British English especially, "thump" is used informally to mean to beat someone very convincingly in a competition or game.

  • Our team thumped the opposition 6–0.
  • She thumped her rival in the final round.
What Makes "Thump" Different From Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it stands apart from its neighbors.

  • Hit — general and neutral. It tells you contact was made, but says nothing about the sound or force.
  • Tap — light, gentle contact. The opposite of thump.
  • Bang — a sharp, loud, crashing sound. A bang is sudden and explosive. A thump is heavier and more muffled.
  • Knock — usually polite or purposeful, like knocking on a door.
  • Pound — similar to thump, but suggests repeated heavy blows, often frantically.
  • Thump — always carries the sense of a single or repeated heavy, dull, solid impact. It has weight to it.

If you drop a feather, it doesn't thump. If you drop a thick encyclopedia, it does.

"Thump" is a physically heavy word — it carries the sensation of force and solidity. When writers use it, they want you to feel the impact, not just read about it. It's vivid and sensory. Whether it's a heart thumping with fear, boots thumping down a hallway, or a fist thumping a table, the word always delivers a sense of weight, force, and that distinctive dull, deep sound.
16012:
A thunderbird is a powerful, supernatural bird from the traditional stories and beliefs of many Indigenous (Native American) peoples of North America. It is not a real bird you can find in nature — it is a mythological being, meaning it exists in the world of spiritual belief, sacred stories, and oral tradition passed down through generations.

The basic idea is this: imagine a bird so enormous and so powerful that when it flaps its wings, it creates the rumbling sound of thunder. When it blinks or flashes its eyes, lightning shoots across the sky. Storms, in many of these traditions, are not just weather events — they are the thunderbird in action.

Different Indigenous nations across North America have their own specific descriptions, but some common features appear again and again:

  • Enormous size — far larger than any real bird. Some traditions say it is large enough to carry a whale or a killer whale in its talons, the way an eagle carries a fish.
  • Bird-like form — typically depicted with a large beak, wings, talons, and feathers, though sometimes with horns or other features.
  • Lightning associations — lightning bolts are often shown coming from its eyes, beak, or the tips of its wings.
  • Great feathers — in some traditions, a single feather from a thunderbird would be an object of immense power.

In the art of Pacific Northwest Coast peoples — such as the Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw, and others — the thunderbird is a very common and recognizable figure. It is often shown at the top of totem poles with its wings spread wide, which is a position of great power and honor.
What Does It Mean? (The Deeper Significance)

The thunderbird is not just a scary monster. In most traditions, it is a protector and a bringer of rain and life. Storms, while dangerous, also bring water to crops and rivers. This dual nature — powerful and destructive, but also life-giving — is central to what the thunderbird represents.

In many Indigenous belief systems, the thunderbird is one of the most important spiritual beings. It occupies a high place in the order of the world, often seen as a guardian that battles evil forces. Some traditions speak of a great eternal conflict between the thunderbird (a sky being) and powerful underwater creatures or serpents (water beings). This battle between sky and water represents the balance of forces in the natural world.

The thunderbird is sacred in many communities. It appears in ceremonies, songs, dances, carvings, and artwork — not as mere decoration, but as a living spiritual presence that people honor and respect.

It is important to understand that "thunderbird" is not a single, uniform legend belonging to one group. Hundreds of distinct Indigenous nations across North America — from the Great Plains to the Pacific Northwest to the Great Lakes region — have their own versions of this being, with their own names, stories, and meanings. When people use the single English word "thunderbird," they are using an umbrella term that covers all of these varied traditions.

For example:

  • The Ojibwe (Great Lakes region) call it Animikiig and regard it as a powerful spirit deeply tied to their spiritual world.
  • The Lakota (Great Plains) have a tradition of the thunderbird as a spirit that brings storms.
  • Pacific Northwest peoples depict it prominently in their visual art and totem culture.

Each of these is distinct, and using the word "thunderbird" flattens those differences into one concept for the sake of a shared English word.

Because of the power and striking image of the thunderbird, the word has been adopted widely in modern American culture as a name for things that want to project strength, speed, and boldness:

  • Ford Thunderbird — a famous American sports car produced by the Ford Motor Company, first made in 1955. It was nicknamed the "T-Bird." The name was chosen to evoke freedom, power, and the spirit of the American road.
  • The Thunderbirds (U.S. Air Force) — the official aerial demonstration team of the United States Air Force, known for flying in precise formations at high speed. They are named after the mythological creature to suggest power and mastery of the skies.
  • Mozilla Thunderbird — a free, open-source email application (software for managing emails on a computer). It was named in a similar spirit to Mozilla Firefox, using a powerful nature-inspired name.
  • Sports teams — many schools, universities, and sports franchises use "Thunderbirds" or "T-Birds" as their team name or mascot, again drawing on the image of power and fierceness.

A thunderbird is a mythological giant bird from Indigenous North American traditions, believed to cause thunder and lightning and to hold great spiritual power. It is a symbol of strength, protection, and the raw force of nature. Its image has become so iconic that in modern times, the word is used to name cars, planes, software, and sports teams — all things meant to suggest power, speed, and impressiveness.

When you see or hear the word "thunderbird," the core image is always the same: something immense, commanding, and electric — rooted in one of the oldest and most widespread legends of the North American continent.
16013:
To understand thunderous, you first need to picture thunder — that enormous, booming sound that rolls across the sky during a storm. It is loud, deep, powerful, and slightly frightening. It doesn't just reach your ears; you can almost feel it in your chest.

Now, thunderous is the adjective built from that image. When you call something thunderous, you are saying it carries the qualities of thunder — its power, its intensity, its loudness, and sometimes even its threatening feeling.

1. Extremely Loud and Deep (The Sound Meaning)

This is the most common use. When a sound is described as thunderous, it means it is so loud, so deep, and so powerful that it resembles a clap of thunder. It is not merely "very loud." It suggests a sound that is overwhelming, earth-shaking, and impossible to ignore.

Think of these situations:

  • A crowd of 80,000 people cheering all at once in a stadium.
  • A massive waterfall crashing onto rocks below.
  • A military jet breaking the sound barrier overhead.
  • An explosion going off in a quarry.

All of these produce sounds that could rightly be called thunderous — sounds that surround you, vibrate through you, and leave no room for anything else.

"The band played its final chord and a thunderous applause filled the entire hall."

Here, the applause wasn't just enthusiastic — it was so powerful and loud that it felt like a physical force, like thunder.

"The old building collapsed with a thunderous crash that woke everyone on the street."

The crash was not a small bang. It was deep, massive, and shook the surroundings.

2. Threatening, Dark, and Angry (The Mood/Expression Meaning)

This is the second — and equally important — meaning. Here, thunderous is not about sound at all. Instead, it describes a look, an expression, or a mood that signals extreme anger, disapproval, or danger — much like how the dark, rumbling sky before a thunderstorm feels threatening and heavy.

"She walked into the room with a thunderous expression on her face."

This does not mean her face was loud. It means her face looked deeply angry, dark, and intimidating — the kind of look that warns everyone around her that something serious is about to happen. Like storm clouds before lightning strikes.

"The manager's thunderous mood silenced the entire office."

Again — no sound involved. His anger and intensity were so palpable and threatening that everyone felt it and went quiet.

What makes thunderous special as a word is that it always carries a sense of raw, uncontrollable power. Whether it is a sound or a mood, something thunderous is not polite, gentle, or subtle. It is dominant, forceful, and commands your full attention.

When a writer uses this word, they want you to feel slightly overwhelmed — just as you would standing in an open field during a thunderstorm.

Thunderous sits at the extreme, intense end of the scale. Consider this ladder for sounds:

Quiet → Loud → Very Loud → Thunderous

And for expressions/moods:

Mildly displeased → Angry → Furious → Thunderous

It is not a mild or moderate word. You would not call a knock on a door thunderous, or call someone slightly irritated thunderous. The word demands something extreme and overwhelming.

In real usage, you will most often see thunderous placed before these words:

  • Thunderous applause — massive, roaring clapping from a crowd
  • Thunderous roar — a huge, deep roaring sound
  • Thunderous crash/explosion — an enormously loud, powerful collision or blast
  • Thunderous expression/look — a face showing deep, threatening anger
  • Thunderous voice — a voice so deep and powerful it fills the room and intimidates
  • Thunderous footsteps — steps so heavy they sound and feel like mini-earthquakes

To sharpen your understanding, here is what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean something is literally thunder or a storm.
  • It does not apply to small or moderate things. A normal sneeze is not thunderous. A slight frown is not thunderous.
  • It does not carry a positive or gentle feeling. Even when used for applause (which is a good thing), it emphasizes the sheer power and scale, not the warmth.
Synonyms — and Why Thunderous Is Unique

Words like deafening, booming, resounding, earsplitting, and roaring share territory with thunderous when describing sound. Words like menacing, dark, furious, and stormy share territory with it when describing a mood.

But thunderous is unique because it combines both worlds in a single word. When you read it, your brain instantly connects to a full sensory experience — the sky darkening, the deep rumble, the vibration, the power. No other word does this quite so efficiently, which is why writers love it.

Thunderous means: having the character of thunder — either in the form of an extremely loud, deep, and powerful sound, or in the form of a dark, threatening, and intensely angry mood or expression.

Whenever you see or use this word, ask yourself: Does this thing feel as powerful, overwhelming, and impossible to ignore as a clap of thunder? If yes — thunderous is exactly the right word.
16014:
When someone is thunderstruck, they are so overwhelmingly shocked, stunned, or astonished by something that they are momentarily frozen — unable to speak, move, or even think clearly. It describes a state where your mind is so blindsided by something unexpected that it simply shuts down for a second, and you are left completely speechless.

Think of it this way: imagine being physically hit by a bolt of lightning. You'd be completely knocked senseless for a moment. Now take that same idea and apply it to your emotions and mind. That's exactly what thunderstruck means — you have been "struck" by news, an event, or a sight so powerful that it hit you like a thunderbolt.
The Intensity: Where Does It Sit?

This is not a gentle word. It lives at the very extreme end of surprise. Consider this scale:

Surprised → Amazed → Shocked → Astonished → Thunderstruck

Saying you were "surprised" means something caught you a little off guard. Saying you were "thunderstruck" means the experience completely overwhelmed you. If you use this word, people will understand that what happened to you was extraordinary, not ordinary.
What It Feels Like From the Inside

When a person is thunderstruck, they typically experience all of the following at once:

Speechlessness. The words just don't come. You open your mouth and nothing happens. Your brain hasn't caught up yet.

Physical stillness. You may stop moving entirely. Your feet feel planted to the floor. You might stare blankly ahead.

Mental overload. Your brain is receiving information it did not at all expect, and it needs a moment — a beat — to process it. In that moment, you are thunderstruck.

A wave of disbelief. Even though something happened right in front of you, part of you cannot believe it is real.
Is It Positive, Negative, or Both?

Here is an important nuance: thunderstruck can be either positive or negative, depending entirely on the situation. The word itself is neutral — it simply describes the overwhelming force of the emotion, not whether the cause is good or bad.

Positive example: A person hears their favourite singer perform live for the first time and the voice is so breathtaking that they stand there, mouth open, thunderstruck by the sheer beauty of it.

Negative example: A woman answers the door to find the police standing there with terrible news about a family member. She is thunderstruck — she cannot speak, cannot move, cannot process what she just heard.

Neutral/mixed example: A man finds out he has been secretly recorded for a years-long surprise documentary about his life. He is thunderstruck — it is not quite bad news, but the shock is immense and total.

In all three cases, the word works perfectly. What ties them together is the overwhelming, sudden, mind-stopping nature of the reaction — not whether it is happy or sad.
It Is Always a Temporary State

Thunderstruck describes the first, immediate moment of shock. It is not a permanent condition. After a person is thunderstruck, they eventually come back to their senses — they begin to cry, laugh, ask questions, or react in some other way. The thunderstruck moment is that brief window right before the reaction kicks in.

• He was thunderstruck when the company announced that he, a junior employee, had been chosen as the new CEO.
  • She stood thunderstruck in the doorway, staring at the birthday party no one had told her about.
  • The whole courtroom fell silent, everyone thunderstruck by the unexpected verdict.
  • I was thunderstruck when my estranged father walked into the room after twenty years.
  • The critics were thunderstruck by the young artist's talent — no one had expected work of such quality.

Notice in each sentence: the cause is always something dramatic and unexpected, and the person experiencing it is always frozen, stunned, and overwhelmed.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Surprised — mild and everyday. You can be surprised by a small gift or a minor coincidence.

Shocked — stronger than surprised; often implies something negative or wrong has happened.

Astonished — very strong wonder and amazement, but the person can usually still function and respond.

Stunned — very close to thunderstruck, but "stunned" often leans slightly more towards numbness and can feel a bit more passive.

Thunderstruck — the most overwhelming of all these. It combines the shock of "shocked," the wonder of "astonished," and the paralysis of "stunned" — all at once, at full force. It is the word you reach for when something truly extraordinary has rendered a person completely powerless in that moment.
A Final Image to Lock It In

Picture someone standing in an open field during a storm. A lightning bolt crashes down right beside them. They are not hurt — but for a second or two, they cannot hear, they cannot think, they cannot move. Every part of them is overwhelmed.

That moment? That is what thunderstruck feels like — but inside your mind, caused not by lightning, but by something utterly unexpected in life.
16015: To thwart something means to stop a plan, effort, goal, or attempt from succeeding — to block or defeat it before it can be completed. But "thwart" is not just any kind of stopping. The essential ingredient is opposition: something was being actively pursued with real intention and energy behind it, and then something else stepped in and defeated it.
What can be thwarted, and by what?

The thing being thwarted is almost always a plan, an attempt, an effort, an ambition, or a goal. You can also thwart a person directly, meaning you stop them from achieving what they're after.

The force doing the thwarting can be a person or group — a detective thwarts a robbery, a rival thwarts your promotion. It can be a situation or natural event — bad weather thwarting a rescue mission, or an illness thwarting an athlete's Olympic dreams. Rules, laws, and systems can thwart people too. What all these share is that the thing being thwarted had real momentum, and something else opposed and defeated it completely.

• The security guard thwarted the thief's escape.
  • Heavy snowfall thwarted the rescue team's efforts.
  • Her plan to surprise her sister was thwarted when her mom accidentally revealed it.
  • The army thwarted the invasion before it could begin.
  • Years of ambition were thwarted by a single bad decision.

Several words are related to "thwart" but carry different meanings. Stop and prevent are neutral — they simply mean something did not happen, with no particular sense of struggle or drama. Hinder and impede mean to slow something down or make it harder, but not to fully defeat it — you can hinder progress without stopping it. Thwart always means the attempt was completely overcome and shut down.

Foil is the closest synonym and can often replace "thwart." The slight difference is that "foil" tends to appear in dramatic, story-like contexts — a hero foils a villain's scheme — while "thwart" is used more broadly across formal writing and general contexts.

Frustrate is broader: it can mean to thwart an effort, or simply to make someone feel annoyed and irritated. "Thwart" is more precise — it always refers to an active effort being fully blocked, not just a feeling.

When something is thwarted, the party whose plan was stopped experiences defeat and disappointment — their effort was cut down before it could succeed. This emotional weight is built into the word itself. Saying something was "thwarted" implies there was a genuine, earnest attempt that met a decisive block.

You'll also see "thwart" used for inner desires and aspirations, not just concrete plans. "Thwarted ambitions," "thwarted love," and "thwarted dreams" are all common phrases. They describe deep goals or desires that were blocked, often by forces outside someone's control — and in these cases, the sense of defeat and lost potential is especially strong.

"Thwart" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs a direct object — something being thwarted. You say "she thwarted his plan" or "they thwarted the attack," never just "she thwarted" on its own. It works naturally in both active and passive voice: The guards thwarted the attack and The attack was thwarted by the guards are both correct and equally common.
Register: when to use this word

"Thwart" is a slightly formal word. You'll encounter it most often in news writing, books, essays, formal reports, and speeches. In casual conversation, most people naturally reach for simpler words like "stopped" or "blocked." That said, "thwart" is not rare or unusual — it's widely understood and used in everyday written English. In your own writing, it's a precise and powerful word to reach for when you want to convey not just that something was stopped, but that it was stopped against a determined, active effort — and stopped decisively.
16016:
When you desperately want something, work toward it, or try very hard to make it happen — and then something or someone completely stops you from getting there — you are thwarted. The word describes the state of being blocked, stopped, or defeated in your effort or desire before it could succeed.

Think of it this way: a river flowing powerfully forward hits a dam and is stopped dead. That river is thwarted. Its force, its direction, its intention — all of it was there, and all of it was stopped.

The adjective can describe two things:

1. A person — someone whose desire, goal, or attempt was prevented from succeeding.

A thwarted lover stands outside the door, unable to reach the person he loves.
The thwarted criminal was arrested before he could rob the bank.

2. A plan, attempt, ambition, or desire — something that was stopped before it could be carried out or fulfilled.

The thwarted escape plan left the prisoners with no hope.
Her thwarted ambitions left a wound that never fully healed.
A thwarted attempt to seize power ended his political career.

Here's what makes "thwarted" richer than a plain word like "stopped" or "blocked."

When something is thwarted, there is almost always an emotional charge attached to it — a sense of frustration, bitterness, or deep disappointment. The word quietly tells you that the person wanted this badly, tried hard, and was then cut off. It carries the weight of that failure.

If I say "his plan was stopped," it's just a fact. If I say "his plan was thwarted," you feel the sting of it — the effort that went nowhere, the goal that was snatched away.

This is why "thwarted" appears so often alongside emotionally heavy words:

  • thwarted ambitions (dreams that were crushed)
  • thwarted desires (deep wants that were never met)
  • thwarted love (romantic pursuit that was blocked or rejected)
  • thwarted villain (someone whose scheme was defeated — often with a sense of drama)

"Thwarted" means the blocking was complete, not partial. It doesn't mean "slightly slowed down" or "made more difficult." It means the effort was stopped in its tracks — the goal was not reached.

A person can be repeatedly thwarted — blocked again and again each time they try — which often builds a deep sense of helplessness or resentment.

Every time she tried to speak up, she was thwarted by those in power.
Nuances That Set It Apart from Similar Words

Thwarted vs. Frustrated:
Both carry a sense of being blocked and emotionally affected. But "frustrated" is more about the internal feeling, while "thwarted" is more about the external blocking — something actively stopped you. You feel frustrated; you are thwarted.

Thwarted vs. Foiled:
Very close in meaning. "Foiled" is often used in slightly dramatic or literary contexts (think comic books: "foiled again!"). "Thwarted" is more natural in everyday serious writing and covers a wider range — it can describe ambitions and emotions, not just schemes and plans.

Thwarted vs. Blocked:
"Blocked" is neutral — a road can be blocked; a drain can be blocked. It carries no emotional weight. "Thwarted" is specifically about effort, desire, or intent being stopped, and it always implies something was at stake for the person involved.

Thwarted vs. Stymied:
"Stymied" means you're stuck and don't know how to move forward — like being baffled. "Thwarted" means something or someone actively stopped you. The source of the problem is different.

These are the most natural combinations you'll encounter or use:

  • thwarted ambitions — life goals that were prevented from being achieved
  • thwarted plans — schemes or arrangements that were stopped before they could be carried out
  • thwarted attempt — an effort that was blocked and did not succeed
  • thwarted desires — wants or cravings that were denied or prevented
  • thwarted efforts — repeated trying that kept being stopped
  • feel thwarted — to feel as though something is constantly blocking you
  • thwarted by circumstances — stopped not by a person but by the situation itself
A Few Sentences to See It in Action

• The thwarted general retreated into bitterness after his campaign was stopped by his own government.
  • Her thwarted desire to study medicine haunted her for the rest of her life.
  • He felt thwarted at every turn — no matter what he tried, something always stood in the way.
  • The detective's investigation, thwarted by lack of evidence, eventually came to a dead end.
  • A thwarted plan to renovate the house left the family living in chaos for months.

Thwarted describes the state of being completely stopped or blocked from achieving what you were trying to do or deeply wanted. It applies to both people (a thwarted artist) and their plans, ambitions, attempts, or desires (thwarted ambitions). Unlike neutral words such as "blocked," "thwarted" carries emotional weight — a quiet sense of frustration, bitterness, or defeat. The blocking is total, not partial, and the word always implies that effort or desire was present before the stopping occurred. It is one of those words that captures not just what happened, but how it felt.
16017: Thyme is a small, low-growing plant used as an herb — meaning it is a plant (or a part of a plant) that people use to add flavour and aroma to food, or for health purposes.

Thyme is a compact, bushy plant with thin, woody stems. Its leaves are extremely small — roughly the size of a sesame seed — oval-shaped, and green on top, slightly pale or silvery underneath. The plant often has tiny flowers, usually lavender, pink, or white, that bloom in small clusters. It grows close to the ground and spreads outward rather than growing tall.

This is one of the most important things to know about thyme. It has a distinctive, strong aroma — warm, earthy, slightly floral, and faintly medicinal. The smell is bold enough that even just brushing your fingers against the plant releases it.

The taste mirrors the smell: warm, savoury, slightly peppery, and a little sharp. It has a mild bitterness in the background. The flavour is strong, so a small amount goes a long way in cooking.
How it is used in cooking

Thyme is one of the most widely used herbs in the world's cuisines. Here is how it appears in the kitchen:

Fresh thyme means the whole sprigs — the stem with tiny leaves attached — are used. You can either strip the leaves off the stem and add just the leaves, or drop the entire sprig into a dish while it cooks and remove the stem before serving.

Dried thyme means the leaves have been removed and dried. The moisture evaporates, which concentrates the flavour, making dried thyme even more intense than fresh.

Thyme works beautifully with:

  • Meats like chicken, lamb, beef, and pork — it is often rubbed onto meat before roasting
  • Soups and stews — a classic addition, as long cooking brings out its depth
  • Vegetables — especially roasted vegetables like potatoes, carrots, and tomatoes
  • Sauces and gravies
  • Breads and marinades

It is a core part of the classic French herb combination called "bouquet garni" (a bundle of herbs tied together and simmered in soups or stews) and "herbes de Provence" (a dried herb mix from southern France).

Importantly, thyme is heat-tolerant — unlike delicate herbs like basil or parsley, it does not lose its flavour when cooked for a long time. This makes it ideal for slow-cooked dishes.
Thyme in traditional and herbal medicine

Beyond cooking, thyme has been used for centuries as a natural remedy. The plant contains a compound called thymol, which has antimicrobial properties — meaning it can fight certain bacteria and fungi. Because of this:

  • Thyme tea or thyme-infused remedies have traditionally been used to soothe coughs, sore throats, and chest congestion
  • It has been used to aid digestion
  • Thyme extract appears in some mouthwashes and antiseptic products (the well-known mouthwash Listerine originally contained thymol)

While these uses are part of herbal tradition and some are supported by research, thyme is not a substitute for medical treatment.

Not all thyme is identical. There are over 300 species of thyme, but the most important ones to know are:

  • Common thyme (Thymus vulgaris) — the standard kitchen thyme, the one you'll find in grocery stores and use in everyday cooking
  • Lemon thyme — a variety with a citrusy, lemony scent layered on top of the classic thyme aroma; popular for fish, chicken, and desserts
  • Wild thyme — a creeping variety that grows naturally across fields and hillsides; less intense in flavour

Thyme is native to the Mediterranean region — think southern France, Italy, Greece, and North Africa — where it grows wild on dry, rocky hillsides in full sun. It thrives in warm, well-drained conditions and is quite hardy. Today it is grown all over the world, both commercially and in home gardens. It is one of the easiest herbs to grow in a pot on a windowsill.

If you want one clear image in your mind: picture a small, slightly scraggly bush barely reaching your ankle, with woody twigs covered in tiny green leaves and a faint purple flower here and there. Rub a pinch of those leaves between your fingers and you get a warm, earthy, almost piney smell. That smell, transferred to your food during cooking, is what thyme is all about.
16018: A tiara is a decorative headpiece — a type of ornamental crown — worn on the head, usually by women. Think of it as a small, elegant, jewel-studded "mini crown." It is considered one of the most glamorous and prestigious accessories a person can wear.

The most important thing to understand about a tiara's shape is that it is not a full circle. It is shaped like an arc or a half-circle — like a wide, curved band that covers only the front and top portion of the head, while the back of the head remains open. It sits on the head like a gentle crown that doesn't close all the way around.

Tiaras are typically made from precious metals like gold, silver, or platinum, and they are studded or decorated with gemstones such as diamonds, pearls, rubies, sapphires, or emeralds. They can be simple and delicate, or extraordinarily elaborate — towering with multiple layers of jewels and fine metalwork. The defining quality is that they are always ornamental — meaning they exist purely for decoration and beauty, not for any practical purpose.
How It Differs from Similar Things

It helps to understand a tiara by comparing it to close cousins:

A crown is a full circular ring that goes all the way around the head. Kings and queens wear crowns. A tiara, by contrast, is open at the back — it is a semi-circle, not a full ring. So while a tiara resembles a crown in spirit, it is architecturally different.

A headband is a simple, everyday item used to hold hair back. A tiara is far more elevated — it is made of precious materials and is worn as a symbol of status, beauty, or celebration, not for a functional hair purpose.

A diadem is a word sometimes used interchangeably with tiara, but traditionally, a diadem refers to a plain, simple band or fillet worn around the head as a symbol of royal or divine authority, while a tiara is more elaborate and jeweled.

Tiaras are worn almost exclusively on formal, celebratory, or ceremonial occasions. You would rarely — if ever — see someone wear a tiara casually.

The most common wearers are:

Royalty and nobility. Queens, princesses, and aristocratic women wear tiaras at state banquets, royal weddings, and formal court events. Famous examples include the tiaras worn by Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana. In royal tradition, tiaras are often priceless heirlooms passed down through generations and carry enormous historical and sentimental weight.

Brides. Many brides choose to wear a tiara on their wedding day as part of their bridal look. It adds a regal, fairytale quality to the occasion.

Beauty pageant winners. When someone wins a major beauty competition — such as Miss Universe or Miss America — a tiara is ceremonially placed on their head as the symbol of their title. The tiara in this context represents honor, achievement, and recognition.

Young girls in play and performance. Tiaras are a popular prop in children's dress-up play, often associated with the idea of being a "princess." They are also worn in dance recitals, theatrical performances, and themed parties.
The Special Case: The Papal Tiara

There is a second, quite different meaning of the word tiara that you must know. The papal tiara (also called the triregnum) is the tall, beehive-shaped, three-tiered crown that was traditionally worn by the Pope — the head of the Roman Catholic Church. This is a very different object from the jeweled women's headpiece described above. It consists of three stacked crowns rising vertically, symbolizing the Pope's three-fold spiritual authority. Although the papal tiara was last used officially by Pope Paul VI in 1964 (and has since been largely set aside), it remains an important symbol of the papacy and still appears in official Catholic heraldry and symbolism.

So when you see "tiara" used in a religious or Catholic context, it almost certainly refers to this papal crown, not the ornamental women's headpiece.
The Bigger Picture: What a Tiara Represents

Beyond just being a physical object, a tiara carries powerful symbolic meaning in human culture. It is universally associated with ideas of royalty, femininity, distinction, celebration, and honor. Placing a tiara on someone's head is a gesture that says, "You are special. You are celebrated. You are being elevated above the ordinary." This is why the image of a tiara appears so frequently in fairy tales, wedding culture, and ceremonies of achievement.

In informal, everyday speech, people sometimes use "tiara" humorously or affectionately — for example, telling someone who is acting self-importantly that they need to "take off their tiara," meaning they should stop acting like royalty.

A tiara is a semi-circular, jeweled ornamental headpiece worn on the front of the head — a glamorous, prestigious object associated with royalty, brides, and winners of great honor. It differs from a crown in that it does not form a complete circle. In a religious context, it can also refer to the Pope's distinctive three-tiered crown. In all its forms, a tiara is a symbol of elevation, celebration, and distinction.
16019: A tic is a sudden, quick, repetitive action — either a movement of the body or a sound — that a person makes without consciously choosing to. It just happens, almost like a glitch the body or voice produces on its own.
The Two Types

Tics fall into two broad categories:

1. Motor tics — involuntary movements. These can include:

  • Blinking rapidly
  • Jerking the head to one side
  • Shrugging the shoulders
  • Scrunching the nose or grimacing
  • Twitching the fingers or arms

2. Vocal tics (also called phonic tics) — involuntary sounds. These can include:

  • Repeatedly clearing the throat
  • Sniffing
  • Grunting
  • In some cases, involuntarily blurting out words or phrases
Simple vs. Complex Tics

Tics also vary by complexity:

  • A simple tic involves only one part of the body or one brief sound — like a single eye blink or a quick grunt.
  • A complex tic involves a coordinated series of movements or sounds — like touching your face, then rolling your eyes, then shrugging, all in a fixed sequence.
The Most Important Thing to Understand: "Involuntary"

The word involuntary here needs careful unpacking, because tics are not quite like other involuntary actions.

If you sneeze, you have zero control over it. Tics are slightly different. Many people with tics describe feeling a building pressure or tension in the body just before a tic — a kind of inner urge — and doing the tic releases that tension. It is a bit like the feeling before you sneeze: you can sometimes hold it back for a little while, but it demands to come out, and suppressing it only makes the urge stronger. Eventually it breaks through.

So while a person can sometimes delay a tic briefly, they cannot simply decide not to have it the way you decide not to scratch your head. The tic is not under meaningful voluntary control. This is why tics are described as semi-voluntary by some doctors — the person is aware of them, but cannot reliably stop them.
Key Characteristics of Tics

To fully understand what makes something a tic (and not just any random movement or sound), look for these features:

  • Sudden — they happen quickly, without a gradual build-up
  • Repetitive — the same action or sound keeps coming back, often in the same form each time
  • Stereotyped — a tic tends to look or sound the same whenever it occurs (your eye-blink tic looks like your eye-blink tic, not a different one each time)
  • Involuntary — not deliberately chosen
  • Temporary — a single tic usually lasts only a fraction of a second to a few seconds
Tics Over Time

Tics are not fixed and permanent. They tend to:

  • Wax and wane — appear more intensely during some periods and fade in others
  • Worsen under stress or excitement — anxiety, nervousness, or even intense focus can trigger more tics
  • Lessen when distracted or absorbed — a person deeply focused on a task may tic less
  • Change over time — a person's tics can shift from one type to another across months or years
Medical Context

Tics are associated with neurological conditions — meaning they come from how the brain is wired, not from a person's personality or willpower. The most well-known condition involving tics is Tourette syndrome, where both motor and vocal tics are present and have lasted for more than a year. However, tics also occur in other conditions and can sometimes appear temporarily in otherwise healthy people, especially children.

It is important to understand that having tics is not a character flaw or a habit someone can break through discipline. Because tics come from the brain, not from choice, treating them like bad habits is both inaccurate and unfair.
The Figurative Use

Outside medicine, the word tic is also used more loosely to describe a small, habitual, recurring quirk in a person's behavior, speech, or creative style — something they keep doing almost without realising it, which becomes a recognisable pattern.

For example:

  • "His conversational tic of saying 'you know what I mean?' after every sentence started to irritate people."
  • "The director's films all share the same tic — a slow-motion shot right before the climax."
  • "She had a tic of tugging at her left ear whenever she was thinking."

In this figurative sense, the action doesn't have to be truly involuntary — it just has to be repeated, characteristic, and mildly unconscious. The person may not even notice they're doing it.
How to Distinguish a Tic from Similar Things

ConceptHow it differs from a tic
HabitA habit is something you once chose and reinforced over time (biting your nails). A tic arises neurologically, not from learning.
Spasm or crampA muscle spasm is a sustained, painful contraction — not quick and repetitive. A tic is brief and doesn't hurt.
SeizureA seizure involves widespread electrical disruption in the brain and usually causes loss of awareness or consciousness. Tics do not impair awareness.
TremorA tremor is a rhythmic, back-and-forth shaking (like in Parkinson's disease). Tics are non-rhythmic, sudden, and can involve the whole body or voice.
In a Sentence

Here are some examples to anchor your understanding:

  • "The child developed a tic — a sudden, repeated sniffing — whenever she was under pressure at school."
  • "His tic of jerking his neck to the right had been with him since childhood."
  • "The author's most recognisable tic is beginning paragraphs with a one-word sentence."
  • "She felt the familiar urge build up and then, involuntarily, blinked hard three times — a tic she had had for years."
The One-Line Summary

A tic is a sudden, repetitive, involuntary movement or sound the body produces — not by choice, but as a neurological impulse — and figuratively, any small, unconscious recurring quirk in a person's behaviour or style.
